clauses.current_legal_basis: Held U.S. Code (release point 119-121, edition through 2026-10-09) prints EO 10199 as a note under 7 U.S.C. 610 with no ending statement, and 7 U.S.C. 610(c) still requires Presidential approval of the Secretary's regulations absent this authorization; the authority act of 1950 is printed by the Code as 3 U.S.C. 301-303 and 3 U.S.C. 301 is held and in force. The bounded eCFR search as of 2026-10-14 and the Federal Register disposition-note search found no revocation or amendment.
clauses.reason: The order authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to make regulations with the force and effect of law, necessary to carry out the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937, without the approval of the President. It has no expiry or condition, no later order held revokes or amends it, and the U.S. Code still prints it as a current note to 7 U.S.C. 610, so it was operative on 2026-10-14.

inventory_overrides.reason: Dossier span 0-1502 contains only EO 10198 (Paul A. Walker exemption); the whole text of EO 10199 (heading and sole paragraph) runs from character 1617 to 2228 of the held text.

research_rationale:
EO 10199 (Truman, signed 1950-12-21, 15 FR 9217, Federal Register of 1950-12-23) is a one-paragraph standing authorization for the Secretary of Agriculture to make regulations under the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937 without the approval of the President. The held text layer prints EO 10198 (Paul A. Walker retirement exemption) immediately before EO 10199 on the same page, so the dossier clause span (characters 0-1502, which holds only the text of EO 10198) is corrected by an inventory override to the EO 10199 heading and operative paragraph. The order has no own-terms end, no later instrument is held that revokes or amends it (Federal Register disposition notes: none), and the U.S. Code (release point 119-121) prints its text as a note under 7 U.S.C. 610 with no ending statement; section 610(c), the provision it relaxes, is still printed in the Code as requiring Presidential approval of the Secretary's regulations, so the order still does work. The authority act of 1950 (Public Law 673) is printed by the Code as sections 301 to 303 of Title 3, and the held text of 3 U.S.C. 301 (added 1951) is in force and covers delegations of functions that require Presidential approval.
